Practice-relevant•Peer-reviewed diagnostic test accuracy systematic review and meta-analysis•October 22, 2026

CSF p-tau181/Aβ42 shows the strongest PET concordance in meta-analysis

Across 38 studies and 7,504 participants, CSF p-tau181/Aβ42 had pooled sensitivity 0.920, specificity 0.884 and bivariate AUC 0.955 against amyloid PET, but heterogeneity and publication bias limit direct implementation.

Key quantitative results: Univariate pooled sensitivity/specificity were 0.920/0.884 for p-tau181/Aβ42, 0.920/0.847 for Aβ42/40, and 0.905/0.875 for t-tau/Aβ42.

BiomarkersCSFAβ42/40p-tau181/Aβ42Amyloid confirmation

Added October 22, 2026 · DOI:10.1007/s40120-026-01056-1

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

All three CSF ratios showed high concordance with amyloid PET. p-tau181/Aβ42 had the highest pooled AUC and lower false-positive rate than Aβ42/40, while overall agreement was similar across ratios. Quantitative PET positivity was associated with lower false-positive rates than visual reading in meta-regression, but that association is not proof that quantification is intrinsically more accurate.

Study design

The authors synthesized 38 studies involving 7,504 participants; 35 studies entered quantitative analyses, representing 28,578 CSF ratio/PET comparisons. Random-effects univariate and bivariate models estimated sensitivity, specificity, false-positive rate and SROC AUC, with meta-regression for assay, population and PET-method moderators. The work was funded by Roche Diagnostics, and the sponsor employed two authors.

Key quantitative results

  • Univariate pooled sensitivity/specificity were 0.920/0.884 for p-tau181/Aβ42, 0.920/0.847 for Aβ42/40, and 0.905/0.875 for t-tau/Aβ42.
  • Bivariate AUC was 0.955 for p-tau181/Aβ42, 0.942 for Aβ42/40, and 0.947 for t-tau/Aβ42; p-tau181/Aβ42 exceeded Aβ42/40 (p=0.018) but not t-tau/Aβ42 at conventional significance (p=0.052).
  • Overall agreement was 90.4% for p-tau181/Aβ42, 89.5% for Aβ42/40 and 89.2% for t-tau/Aβ42.
  • PET positivity defined by SUVR or Centiloid was associated with lower false-positive rates than visual reading in meta-regression (p<0.0001 and p=0.0051, respectively).
  • Publication-bias asymmetry was detected for sensitivity (p<0.0001), potentially inflating pooled sensitivity and SROC estimates.

What changed

The final peer-reviewed meta-analysis expands the evidence base beyond the earlier conference abstract and directly compares the three principal CSF ratio families against amyloid PET.

Strength of evidence

Moderate-to-strong synthesis-level clinical-validity evidence because it includes 38 studies and multiple automated platforms. Confidence in exact pooled estimates is reduced by heterogeneity, publication-bias signals, study-quality variation, specialist/research sampling and differing PET reference methods.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

CSF ratios remain strong alternatives to amyloid PET for confirming amyloid pathology. Ratio selection should still follow locally validated assay cutoffs and intended use; the small pooled differences do not establish universal interchangeability or patient-outcome utility.

Field medical relevance

Directly informs CSF–PET concordance, ratio selection, platform interpretation, PET reference methods and the limits of applying pooled diagnostic accuracy to an individual laboratory.

Quanterix or platform relevance

Elecsys and Lumipulse supplied 80.7% of the 28,578 biomarker/PET comparisons, but studies used different assays, cutoffs, tracers and PET reading methods. Pooled ratios rank evidence across heterogeneous implementations rather than establishing interchangeable cutoffs.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The synthesis supports diagnostic alternatives but creates no authorization, availability, coverage or reimbursement change. Local CSF access, PET access and payer rules remain separate questions.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Is p-tau181/Aβ42 definitively superior to every other CSF ratio?
It had the highest pooled AUC and outperformed Aβ42/40, but the difference from t-tau/Aβ42 narrowly missed conventional significance and study heterogeneity prevents a universal ranking.
Does quantitative PET prove a better truth standard than visual reading?
No. Meta-regression found lower false-positive rates with SUVR or Centiloid definitions, but cross-study confounding prevents a causal accuracy conclusion.
Can the pooled results determine a laboratory cutoff?
No. Assay- and laboratory-specific validated cutoffs remain necessary.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Substantial heterogeneity across assays, cutoffs, tracers and PET reading methods
  • Mostly specialist, research and trial cohorts
  • Publication-bias signal for sensitivity
  • Risk-of-bias variation across included studies
  • No direct patient-outcome or decision-impact evidence
  • Roche funded the review and employed two authors

Primary source · DOI

Martinez-Lage P, Solje E, Martins JG, et al. Cerebrospinal Fluid Biomarker Ratio Concordance with Amyloid Positron-Emission Tomography: A Diagnostic Test Accuracy Meta-analysis. Neurol Ther. Published online October 22, 2026. doi:10.1007/s40120-026-01056-1.

Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed cross-sectional and longitudinal cohort analysis•October 21, 2026

p-tau217/PET discordance has direction-specific meaning

Across 1,069 cognitively normal adults, plasma p-tau217-positive/PET-negative and p-tau217-negative/PET-positive profiles carried different biomarker and longitudinal signals, and the p-tau217 operating point changed their interpretation.

Key quantitative results: The combined analysis included 1,069 cognitively normal adults: 594 in CPAS and 475 in ADNI.

BiomarkersBloodp-tau217Aβ42/40Discordance interpretation

Added October 22, 2026 · DOI:10.1002/alz.71922; PMID:42902436

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Discordance was not a single intermediate state. p-tau217-positive/PET-negative participants had higher GFAP and NfL, whereas p-tau217-negative/PET-positive participants showed lower plasma Aβ42/40 in ADNI. Both p-tau217-positive groups had greater clinical-progression risk, while both PET-positive groups accumulated amyloid faster. The p-tau217-positive/PET-negative accumulation signal appeared only with less-specific cutoffs, underscoring that assay operating points shape discordance.

Study design

Investigators analyzed 594 cognitively normal adults from CPAS and 475 from ADNI. Amyloid PET positivity was defined as at least 20 Centiloids; cohort-specific p-tau217 cutoffs were anchored to PET at at least 90% specificity. Cross-sectional plasma, imaging and cognitive profiles were compared across four concordance groups, with mixed-effects and Cox models applied to longitudinal ADNI imaging, cognition and clinical progression.

Key quantitative results

  • The combined analysis included 1,069 cognitively normal adults: 594 in CPAS and 475 in ADNI.
  • Relative to p-tau217-negative/PET-negative participants, the p-tau217-positive/PET-negative group had higher GFAP and NfL in both cohorts, while the p-tau217-negative/PET-positive group had lower plasma Aβ42/40 in ADNI.
  • In ADNI, both p-tau217-positive groups had higher clinical-progression risk and faster decline in selected cognitive domains; both PET-positive groups showed faster Centiloid accumulation.
  • Faster Centiloid accumulation in the p-tau217-positive/PET-negative group was observed only when lower-specificity p-tau217 thresholds were used.

What changed

The publication separates the two directions of p-tau217/PET discordance and demonstrates that their biological and prognostic meaning depends partly on the chosen p-tau217 operating point.

Strength of evidence

Moderate clinical-validity evidence from two sizable cohorts, strengthened by longitudinal ADNI follow-up. Clinical utility remains unproven because thresholds were cohort-specific, outcome effects were observational, and no discordance-guided clinical decision strategy was tested.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

A discordant result should be interpreted by direction, assay and cutoff rather than labeled generically as uncertain. Consequential results still require clinical correlation and confirmatory amyloid testing when definitive pathology status is needed.

Field medical relevance

Directly addresses blood–PET concordance, cutoff selection, sequential testing and the distinction between risk enrichment and confirmed amyloid pathology.

Quanterix or platform relevance

p-tau217 positivity used cohort-specific PET-anchored cutoffs selected for at least 90% specificity. The study therefore evaluates operating-point-dependent discordance rather than establishing a transferable assay cutoff.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No authorization, availability, reimbursement or coverage change. The findings refine interpretation rather than creating an ordering pathway.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does p-tau217-positive/PET-negative mean early amyloid accumulation?
Not reliably. Faster Centiloid accumulation in that group appeared only at lower-specificity p-tau217 thresholds, so the interpretation depends on the assay operating point and may also reflect non-amyloid injury signals.
Does a discordant blood result replace amyloid PET?
No. The study supports direction-specific risk interpretation but explicitly requires validation before clinical use and does not establish a replacement rule.
Can these cutoffs be transferred to another assay?
No. Positivity was defined with cohort-specific PET-anchored cutoffs, not universal concentrations.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Cognitively normal cohorts limit generalizability to symptomatic specialty care
  • Cohort-specific p-tau217 assays and cutoffs
  • Longitudinal analyses were available in ADNI rather than both cohorts
  • The abstract does not provide absolute event rates or model effect estimates
  • No prospective test of discordance-guided clinical management

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Huang Y, Huang L, Cui L, et al. Direction-specific biomarker profiles and clinical significance of plasma p-tau217/amyloid PET discordance in cognitively normal adults. Alzheimers Dement. 2026;22(10):e71922. doi:10.1002/alz.71922.

Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed diagnostic-accuracy and threshold study•October 21, 2026

Automated p-tau217 dual cutoffs leave an 11.9% gray zone

In 135 Taiwanese memory-clinic participants, cohort-derived Roche Elecsys p-tau217 cutoffs below 0.225 and above 0.336 pg/mL classified 88.1% into definitive zones with 95.0% agreement inside those zones.

Key quantitative results: In the 135-person primary analysis, Roche p-tau217 achieved AUC 0.973. A single 0.251 pg/mL cutoff yielded 93.2% positive agreement, 89.5% negative agreement and 91.1% overall agreement.

BiomarkersBloodp-tau217p-tau181Amyloid triage

Added October 22, 2026 · DOI:10.1007/s00415-026-14193-2

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The automated assay showed high discrimination and a relatively small intermediate zone, but its apparent threshold performance was derived and evaluated in one cohort. Roche and Simoa p-tau217 AUCs were not significantly different in complete cases, while both outperformed p-tau181 and NfL. Lower eGFR raised p-tau217 concentrations, and advanced kidney disease was not represented.

Study design

The study enrolled 139 adults from a Taiwanese memory clinic; 136 had florbetaben PET and three had CSF reference testing. Four extreme statistical values were excluded from the primary threshold analysis, leaving 76 amyloid-negative and 59 amyloid-positive participants. Single and dual cutoffs were derived within that same cohort, and 81 complete cases contributed to head-to-head biomarker comparisons.

Key quantitative results

  • In the 135-person primary analysis, Roche p-tau217 achieved AUC 0.973. A single 0.251 pg/mL cutoff yielded 93.2% positive agreement, 89.5% negative agreement and 91.1% overall agreement.
  • Dual cutoffs below 0.225 and above 0.336 pg/mL placed 119/135 participants (88.1%) in definitive zones and 16/135 (11.9%) in the intermediate zone; agreement within definitive zones was 95.0% (95% CI, 89.3%–98.1%).
  • Among 81 complete cases, Roche p-tau217 AUC was 0.970 versus 0.957 for Simoa p-tau217 (p=0.097), 0.880 for Roche p-tau181 (p=0.010) and 0.615 for Roche NfL (p<0.001).
  • Lower eGFR was independently associated with higher p-tau217 concentrations (B=-0.012, p=0.002), but only seven participants had moderate CKD and none had severe CKD.

What changed

The study supplies East Asian memory-clinic data on an automated p-tau217 platform, quantifies a cohort-derived dual-cutoff gray zone, and reports direct assay comparisons and renal-function effects.

Strength of evidence

Moderate clinical-validity evidence. Reference testing was strong for most participants and head-to-head comparisons were blinded, but the single-center sample was modest, thresholds were derived and evaluated in the same cohort, and advanced kidney disease and clinical utility were not tested.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The results support further validation of automated p-tau217 triage, not immediate adoption of the published concentrations. Values near a threshold, discordant presentations, treatment-eligibility decisions and advanced CKD still require confirmatory evaluation.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to platform comparison, dual cutoffs, gray-zone size, non-Western validation, renal confounding and confirmatory-testing workflows.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The study directly compared automated Roche p-tau217 with Simoa p-tau217 and derived assay-specific candidate decision zones. The thresholds differ from FDA-cleared U.S. labeling and cannot be transferred without external validation.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No new authorization, availability, reimbursement or coverage. The study informs implementation research but does not alter local access to the assay or confirmatory PET/CSF.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Are 0.225 and 0.336 pg/mL clinical cutoffs?
No. They were derived in this cohort and differ from U.S. FDA-cleared labeling; independent validation is required.
Did Roche outperform Simoa p-tau217?
No statistically significant AUC difference was detected in 81 complete cases (0.970 vs 0.957; p=0.097).
Does kidney function matter?
Lower eGFR was associated with higher concentrations, but discrimination did not improve significantly when eGFR was added and severe CKD was not studied.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Single-center cross-sectional design
  • Modest sample and only 59 amyloid-positive participants in the primary analysis
  • Thresholds were derived and evaluated in the same cohort
  • Only 81 complete cases contributed to head-to-head comparisons
  • Only seven participants had moderate CKD and none had severe CKD
  • No prospective decision-impact or patient-outcome study

Primary source · DOI

Lin YS, Tsai MJ, Lai CL, et al. Clinical performance and decision thresholds of an automated plasma p-tau217 assay for amyloid pathology in a Taiwanese memory clinic. J Neurol. 2026;273:674. doi:10.1007/s00415-026-14193-2.

Practice-relevant•Peer-reviewed retrospective real-world diagnostic-impact study•October 20, 2026

Plasma p-tau217 changes etiologic classification in a memory clinic

In 98 evaluable memory-clinic patients, adding plasma p-tau217 or PrecivityAD2 changed the AD versus non-AD etiologic classification in 37.8% using a 0.18 p-tau217 threshold and 46.9% using a 0.325 threshold.

Key quantitative results: Overall reclassification was 37.8% with the lower threshold (p=0.001) and 46.9% with the higher threshold (p<0.001).

BiomarkersBloodp-tau217Aβ42/40Etiologic diagnosis

Added October 20, 2026 · DOI:10.1097/WAD.0000000000000761

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Biomarker disclosure frequently changed clinicians' AD versus non-AD etiologic impression, especially with the higher p-tau217 threshold and among APOE ε4 noncarriers. The direction was usually away from AD, but final diagnoses were biomarker-informed and not independently verified, so reclassification should not be equated with improved diagnostic accuracy.

Study design

A tertiary memory clinic retrospectively reviewed 100 patients aged at least 50 years who had been assessed with clinical evaluation, neuropsychological testing, and MRI before blood-biomarker results were available. Ninety-eight had evaluable Labcorp Lumipulse p-tau217 (n=75) or PrecivityAD2 (n=23) testing. Multidisciplinary diagnoses before and after biomarker disclosure were compared using a lower p-tau217 threshold greater than 0.18 and a higher threshold greater than 0.325; PrecivityAD2 used manufacturer APS2 categories.

Key quantitative results

  • Overall reclassification was 37.8% with the lower threshold (p=0.001) and 46.9% with the higher threshold (p<0.001).
  • At the higher threshold, 55.3% of 76 initially AD-classified patients shifted to non-AD, while 18.2% of initially non-AD patients shifted to AD.
  • Among APOE ε4 carriers, higher-threshold changes were balanced: 42% AD-to-non-AD versus 43% non-AD-to-AD (p=0.096).
  • Among APOE ε4 noncarriers, higher-threshold changes were asymmetric: 66% AD-to-non-AD versus 14% non-AD-to-AD (p<0.001).

What changed

The final peer-reviewed report supplies real-world evidence that plasma biomarker results can materially alter etiologic classification and that the size and direction of that effect depend on the interpretation threshold.

Strength of evidence

Moderate decision-impact evidence from routine specialist practice, weakened by retrospective single-center design, use of two different assays, and lack of uniform independent amyloid confirmation. It demonstrates changed decisions, not that the changed decisions were correct or improved outcomes.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Threshold choice can shift many patients away from an AD label. Clinicians should treat p-tau217 as one part of a full evaluation and confirm discordant or consequential results rather than assuming that a reclassification rate proves diagnostic utility.

Field medical relevance

Useful for MSL discussions about clinical utility, threshold sensitivity, assay-specific interpretation, APOE context, and the difference between diagnostic reclassification and validated diagnostic correctness.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The analysis combined a standalone Lumipulse p-tau217 result with PrecivityAD2, then evaluated two p-tau217 thresholds. Because the assays and interpretation rules were not uniform and no common PET or CSF reference standard was applied, the study measures decision impact rather than comparative analytical or diagnostic accuracy.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No authorization or coverage change. The study shows potential diagnostic workflow impact but does not establish payer acceptance or access to confirmatory testing.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does a changed diagnosis mean the biomarker improved accuracy?
Not necessarily. Final diagnoses incorporated the biomarker and were not uniformly verified against PET, CSF, or neuropathology.
Can the 0.18 and 0.325 cutoffs be applied to every p-tau217 assay?
No. They were tied to the Labcorp Lumipulse workflow and should not be transferred to other assays without validation.
Why did the higher threshold move more patients away from AD?
A more stringent positive threshold classified more low or intermediate results as not supportive of AD, increasing AD-to-non-AD reclassification.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Retrospective single-center tertiary-clinic design
  • Only 98 evaluable patients
  • Two different blood-biomarker workflows were combined
  • No uniform amyloid PET, CSF, or neuropathologic reference standard
  • Simplified AD versus non-AD categories may obscure mixed pathology
  • No patient-outcome or prospective utility assessment

Primary source · DOI · Public study manuscript

Maerean N, Litchev S, Jackson GR, Kass JS, Pavlik VN, Lin CYR. Plasma Phosphorylated Tau 217 Reshapes Diagnostic Classification in a Real-World Memory Clinic Cohort. Alzheimer Dis Assoc Disord. Published online October 20, 2026. doi:10.1097/WAD.0000000000000761.

Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed model development and external-validation study•October 19, 2026

Two-stage p-tau217 reflex testing reduces the modeled PET gray zone

In external validation among 1,644 A4/LEARN participants, a p-tau217 gatekeeper followed by a multimarker reflex model improved gray-zone AUC from 0.719 to 0.793, reduced PET referral from 35.9% to 24.3%, and classified 90.7% without PET.

Key quantitative results: Full-model AUC was 0.915 (95% CI, 0.859–0.961) in ADNI and 0.879 (95% CI, 0.861–0.895) in external A4/LEARN validation.

BiomarkersBloodp-tau217Aβ42/40Sequential testing

Added October 20, 2026 · DOI:10.1002/acn3.70560; PMID:42897700

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

GRAD routes a p-tau217 probability of 0.25 to 0.75 to a reflex model using p-tau217, Aβ42/40, GFAP, APOE ε4, age, and a tau-amyloid divergence term. External gray-zone discrimination improved and modeled PET use fell, but calibration shifted across cohorts and the reflex stage alone did not meet recommended performance for replacing amyloid PET.

Study design

Investigators developed the two-stage GRAD algorithm in 145 cognitively impaired ADNI participants and externally validated the locked model in 1,644 cognitively unimpaired A4/LEARN participants. Amyloid PET was the reference standard: florbetapir SUVR greater than 1.11 in ADNI and at least 20 Centiloids in A4/LEARN. Probabilities below 0.25 or above 0.75 were resolved by p-tau217 alone; the gray zone entered an L2-regularized multimarker model.

Key quantitative results

  • Full-model AUC was 0.915 (95% CI, 0.859–0.961) in ADNI and 0.879 (95% CI, 0.861–0.895) in external A4/LEARN validation.
  • Among 630 external gray-zone participants, the reflex model improved AUC from 0.719 with p-tau217 alone to 0.793 (p<0.001), increased correct classification without PET from 41.4% to 56.2%, and reduced PET referral from 35.9% to 24.3%.
  • Overall, 89.0% of ADNI and 90.7% of A4/LEARN participants were classified without PET. External sensitivity was 76.7%, specificity 88.6%, PPV 93.9%, and NPV 62.3%.
  • Calibration did not fully transfer: the external intercept was +0.93, with mean predicted risk 57.5% versus observed amyloid prevalence 69.6%.
  • Modeled testing costs were 44%–52% lower than p-tau217 screening followed by PET for every gray-zone result; this was an economic simulation, not a prospective utilization study.

What changed

A peer-reviewed, externally tested reflex architecture now quantifies how a second blood-based stage can shrink the p-tau217 gray zone while preserving PET for residual uncertainty.

Strength of evidence

Moderate-to-strong clinical-validity evidence because the model was locked and externally validated against amyloid PET in a large independent cohort. Clinical utility remains unproven because routing decisions, patient outcomes, and real-world costs were modeled rather than prospectively tested.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The findings support reflex testing as a research and implementation strategy, not a replacement for confirmatory imaging. The external calibration shift, 62.3% NPV, and below-replacement performance of the reflex stage require local validation before individual treatment or enrollment decisions.

Field medical relevance

Directly addresses common MSL questions about p-tau217 gray zones, sequential testing, cross-platform transport, residual PET demand, prevalence effects, and the distinction between discrimination and calibration.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The model was developed with Lumipulse and Janssen p-tau217 measurements and transported to Lilly MSD p-tau217, with platform harmonization based on cohort-specific reference distributions. The cross-platform result is encouraging, but the thresholds are not directly transferable laboratory cutoffs and require setting-specific calibration.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The workflow could reduce confirmatory PET demand if prospectively validated, but the publication creates no new authorization, availability, reimbursement, coverage, or ordering pathway.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does GRAD replace amyloid PET?
No. The authors retain PET for residual uncertainty, and the external reflex stage achieved 66.7% sensitivity and 80.0% specificity, below the recommended benchmark for replacing PET.
Are the 0.25 and 0.75 values laboratory concentration cutoffs?
No. They are model probabilities after platform harmonization, not transferable pg/mL cutoffs.
Did the cost savings occur in clinical practice?
No. Costs were modeled using cohort routing rates and assumed unit prices.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Small development cohort and only 49 development gray-zone cases
  • External cohort was cognitively unimpaired, unlike the cognitively impaired development cohort
  • Cross-platform harmonization used cohort-specific reference distributions
  • External calibration shifted materially
  • No prospective clinical-utility, decision-impact, or health-system implementation trial
  • Cost results depend on assumed prices and modeled routing

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Parankusham H, Vanderlip C, Birkenbihl C, et al. A Two-Stage Plasma Biomarker Algorithm Reduces Amyloid PET Use and the p-Tau217 Gray Zone. Ann Clin Transl Neurol. Published online October 19, 2026. doi:10.1002/acn3.70560.

Practice-relevant•Peer-reviewed multicenter real-world treatment registry•October 19, 2026

Korean registry quantifies real-world lecanemab ARIA and early PET clearance

Among 663 lecanemab-treated patients at 32 Korean hospitals, ARIA occurred in 16.1%, symptomatic ARIA-E in 0.6%, and baseline superficial siderosis was associated with a 7.45-fold higher hazard of ARIA-E.

Key quantitative results: ARIA occurred in 106/657 patients (16.1%): ARIA-E with or without ARIA-H in 27 (4.1%) and isolated ARIA-H in 79 (12.0%). Four patients (0.6%) had symptomatic ARIA-E.

ManagementMRIARIA-EARIA-HTreatment safety monitoring

Added October 20, 2026 · DOI:10.1186/s13195-026-02232-z; JOY-ALZ registry

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The largest same-window real-world report provides actionable rates and risk associations for lecanemab safety. ARIA-E clustered with APOE ε4 homozygosity, worse baseline CDR-SB, microhemorrhages, and superficial siderosis. Clinician-selected dose titration reduced infusion reactions but did not show lower ARIA within genotype strata, so the observational data do not establish a safer off-label dosing strategy.

Study design

JOY-ALZ analyzed 663 patients with Alzheimer disease who received at least one lecanemab infusion across 32 hospitals. ARIA analyses included 657 patients with at least one monitoring MRI. Clinicians used dose titration selectively, and exploratory analyses related genotype, clinical status, baseline MRI markers, plasma p-tau217, and amyloid PET to safety and short-term outcomes.

Key quantitative results

  • ARIA occurred in 106/657 patients (16.1%): ARIA-E with or without ARIA-H in 27 (4.1%) and isolated ARIA-H in 79 (12.0%). Four patients (0.6%) had symptomatic ARIA-E.
  • ARIA-E was associated with APOE ε4 homozygosity (HR 2.81; 95% CI, 1.06–7.46), higher baseline CDR-SB (HR 1.18 per point; 95% CI, 1.04–1.35), more baseline microhemorrhages (HR 1.69; 95% CI, 1.32–2.16), and baseline superficial siderosis (HR 7.45; 95% CI, 1.50–37.12).
  • Infusion-related reactions occurred in 26.7% and were less frequent with dose titration, but ARIA-E and ARIA-H did not differ between standard and titration groups within APOE genotype strata.
  • MMSE declined by 0.15 points per month (95% CI, −0.21 to −0.08; p<0.001). Higher baseline plasma p-tau217 was associated with greater worsening in functional activities.
  • Amyloid PET became negative in 15/64 (23.4%) at 3–9 months and 8/29 (27.6%) at 10–12 months; lower baseline Centiloid (OR 0.92; 95% CI, 0.88–0.96) and higher baseline MMSE (OR 1.23; 95% CI, 1.04–1.45) were associated with negativity.

What changed

The multicenter registry supplies large-scale routine-care estimates for ARIA, infusion reactions, MRI risk factors, and early PET clearance under lecanemab outside a randomized trial.

Strength of evidence

Moderate real-world safety evidence from a large multicenter registry. Treatment, titration, MRI, and follow-up were not randomized; clinical and PET follow-up were short; and PET analyses involved small subsets, limiting efficacy and causal dosing conclusions.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Baseline superficial siderosis and microhemorrhage burden reinforced ARIA-E risk stratification, while symptomatic ARIA-E was uncommon. The data support careful label-based selection and MRI monitoring but do not justify changing dose or surveillance schedules.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to MSL discussions about real-world ARIA rates, APOE and MRI risk, dose titration, early PET response, and the difference between observational association and a validated monitoring strategy.

Quanterix or platform relevance

MRI markers were evaluated as ARIA-E risk factors, while small PET subsets were used to characterize early amyloid clearance. The study informs monitoring interpretation but does not validate an alternative MRI schedule, PET stopping rule, or p-tau217 response threshold.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No authorization, availability, reimbursement, or coverage change. The multicenter experience may inform implementation capacity but does not create a new access pathway.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Did dose titration reduce ARIA?
Not within APOE genotype strata. It was associated with fewer infusion reactions, but the nonrandomized analysis does not establish an ARIA-prevention effect.
Which baseline features were most strongly associated with ARIA-E?
Superficial siderosis had HR 7.45, APOE ε4 homozygosity HR 2.81, and each additional baseline microhemorrhage HR 1.69, with wide confidence intervals for some estimates.
Can early PET negativity guide stopping treatment?
No. PET data came from small observational subsets, and the study did not validate a stopping rule.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Observational registry without randomized dosing or comparator group
  • Clinician-selected dose titration creates confounding by indication
  • Short clinical follow-up
  • Small amyloid-PET follow-up subsets
  • Potential variation in routine-care imaging and outcome assessment
  • No validated treatment-stopping or biomarker-guided dosing rule

Primary source · DOI

Kang SH, Jeong JH, Lim JS, et al. Safety, short-term clinical outcomes, and associated factors of lecanemab: a multicenter real-world study from the Korean Joint Registry for Alzheimer's Treatment and Diagnostics (JOY-ALZ). Alzheimers Res Ther. Published online October 19, 2026. doi:10.1186/s13195-026-02232-z.

Practice-relevant•Peer-reviewed retrospective real-world treatment cohort•October 17, 2026

Baseline MRI markers stratify anti-amyloid outcomes and ARIA-H risk

In a 161-patient real-world anti-amyloid cohort, severe medial-temporal atrophy predicted greater 12-month functional worsening during lecanemab, while baseline microbleeds were associated with a 14-fold higher odds of ARIA-H across lecanemab and donanemab treatment.

Key quantitative results: With lecanemab, mean CDR-SB worsened by 0.79 points at six months, 1.10 at 12 months and 1.60 at 18 months.

BiomarkersManagementMRIMedial temporal atrophyCerebral microbleedsTreatment prognostication

Added October 18, 2026 · DOI:10.1016/j.tjpad.2026.100686; PMID:42892274

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The cohort separates two baseline MRI questions. Medial-temporal atrophy was associated with subsequent functional decline during lecanemab, while pre-existing microbleeds strongly enriched ARIA-H risk across treated patients. Amyloid-PET burden was not consistently associated with outcomes. These associations may improve counseling and risk discussions, but the retrospective design does not prove that changing treatment based on either marker improves outcomes.

Study design

Investigators retrospectively followed 161 consecutive patients initiating anti-amyloid therapy at a Tokyo dementia center from 2024 to 2026: 89 received lecanemab and 72 received donanemab. Baseline medial-temporal atrophy was quantified with a VSRAD Z score, amyloid-PET burden and cerebral microbleeds were recorded, and associations with MMSE, CDR-SB and ARIA were evaluated. Lecanemab follow-up extended to 18 months; donanemab follow-up was limited to six months.

Key quantitative results

  • With lecanemab, mean CDR-SB worsened by 0.79 points at six months, 1.10 at 12 months and 1.60 at 18 months.
  • Greater baseline medial-temporal atrophy correlated with greater 12-month CDR-SB worsening (r=0.39, p=0.01; n=40). Patients with severe atrophy, defined as VSRAD Z score at least 3, worsened by 2.62 versus 0.64 CDR-SB points (adjusted beta=+2.18, p<0.001).
  • ARIA-H occurred in 6 of 25 patients with baseline microbleeds versus 3 of 136 without microbleeds, corresponding to an odds ratio of 14.0 (p<0.001). All observed ARIA events were asymptomatic.
  • Baseline amyloid-PET burden showed no significant association with clinical outcomes at most time points.

What changed

This newly published real-world cohort quantifies how baseline atrophy and microbleeds relate to different downstream questions: expected functional course and hemorrhagic ARIA risk during routine anti-amyloid treatment.

Strength of evidence

Moderate real-world prognostic and safety evidence from 161 consecutive treated patients with structured MRI and clinical follow-up. The retrospective single-center design, small 12-month atrophy-outcome subset, limited donanemab follow-up and lack of an untreated comparator prevent causal treatment-effect or clinical-utility conclusions.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Baseline microbleeds remain an important ARIA-H risk signal, while severe medial-temporal atrophy may identify patients likely to decline despite treatment. Neither finding independently establishes a contraindication or a reason to stop therapy; drug labeling, MRI criteria and individualized benefit-risk assessment remain controlling.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to MSL discussions about MRI eligibility, prognostic counseling, ARIA risk, differences between safety and efficacy markers, and what real-world baseline imaging can and cannot establish.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The central analysis evaluates whether baseline MRI markers add prognostic or safety information during anti-amyloid treatment. It supports interpretation of medial-temporal atrophy and microbleeds as risk markers, but does not validate a new automated threshold, replace label-based MRI eligibility criteria, or establish interchangeability across MRI acquisition and analysis methods.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No authorization, availability, reimbursement or coverage change. The study may inform counseling and MRI interpretation but does not expand access or create a new monitoring requirement.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does severe medial-temporal atrophy mean anti-amyloid treatment should not be offered?
No. Severe atrophy was associated with greater functional worsening in an observational subgroup, but the study did not test a treatment-withholding rule or demonstrate that atrophy modifies treatment benefit versus no treatment.
Do baseline microbleeds predict ARIA-H?
Yes, within this cohort: ARIA-H occurred in 6/25 patients with microbleeds and 3/136 without, for an odds ratio of 14.0. The estimate should still be interpreted with the small event count and existing label-based MRI criteria.
Did amyloid-PET burden predict clinical outcomes?
Not consistently. Baseline PET burden showed no significant association at most assessed time points.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Retrospective single-center design
  • No untreated or matched comparator
  • Only 40 lecanemab-treated patients contributed to the 12-month atrophy-outcome correlation
  • Only nine ARIA-H events produced the microbleed risk estimate
  • Donanemab follow-up was limited to six months
  • No prospective test of a marker-guided treatment decision

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Kujuro Y, Saito M, Maruko M, et al. Baseline MRI markers and clinical outcomes during anti-amyloid beta therapy: A real-world study in a Japanese dementia center. J Prev Alzheimers Dis. Published online October 17, 2026. doi:10.1016/j.tjpad.2026.100686.

Important new evidence•Peer-reviewed post-hoc biomarker analysis of phase 3 trial data•October 16, 2026

Baseline amyloid burden predicts one-year donanemab PET clearance

In a TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 post-hoc analysis, lower baseline amyloid was the strongest predictor of reaching less than 24.1 Centiloids at week 52; amyloid-clear and non-clear subgroups had similar CDR-SB slowing, while tau-PET slowing was significant only after clearance.

Key quantitative results: Among evaluable donanemab-treated participants, 443 reached less than 24.1 Centiloids at week 52 and 227 did not. Mean baseline amyloid was 95.8 versus 120.2 Centiloids; week-52 means were 4.8 versus 48.2 Centiloids, respectively (p<0.001).

BiomarkersAmyloid PETAmyloid CentiloidTau PETTreatment response monitoring

Added October 16, 2026 · DOI:10.1186/s13195-026-02163-9; NCT04437511

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Amyloid clearance at one year was most strongly related to starting amyloid burden, followed by age, APOE ε4 count and body weight. Clearance was associated with slower tau accumulation and a larger p-tau217 change, but clinical slowing was observed whether or not the PET threshold was reached. The analysis is exploratory and does not prove that forcing every patient below 24.1 Centiloids improves outcomes.

Study design

Investigators analyzed TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 randomized data (876 placebo; 860 donanemab) and an open-label addendum (1,053 participants). Donanemab-treated participants with evaluable week-52 PET were classified as amyloid-clear below 24.1 Centiloids or non-clear at 24.1 Centiloids or higher. Baseline predictors were assessed with machine learning and regression; propensity-matched placebo comparisons evaluated downstream biomarkers and clinical outcomes.

Key quantitative results

  • Among evaluable donanemab-treated participants, 443 reached less than 24.1 Centiloids at week 52 and 227 did not. Mean baseline amyloid was 95.8 versus 120.2 Centiloids; week-52 means were 4.8 versus 48.2 Centiloids, respectively (p<0.001).
  • Lower baseline amyloid was the most important predictor of clearance, followed by older age, fewer APOE ε4 alleles and lower body weight; baseline amyloid was inversely associated with clearance probability (p<0.001).
  • At week 76, only the amyloid-clear subgroup had significantly less tau accumulation than matched placebo (p<0.01). Both subgroups had significant plasma p-tau217 differences from matched placebo, with a larger change after clearance.
  • CDR-SB progression slowing versus matched placebo was 29.6% in the clear subgroup and 28.8% in the non-clear subgroup; iADRS slowing was 25.9% and 18.8%, respectively.

What changed

The analysis quantifies which baseline features predict one-year PET clearance and separates the relationship between clearance, downstream tau/p-tau217 change and clinical outcomes in a large phase 3 population.

Strength of evidence

Large trial-derived dataset with replication in an open-label addendum and quantitative PET, plasma and clinical outcomes. Causal interpretation is limited by post-hoc subgrouping, incomplete week-52 PET availability and propensity matching rather than randomized comparison between clearance states.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Starting amyloid burden influences the chance of crossing the 24.1-Centiloid threshold by one year. Failure to cross that threshold did not eliminate observed clinical slowing, so a single PET threshold should not be interpreted as an individual clinical-response rule without label- and pathway-specific evidence.

Field medical relevance

Directly relevant to MSL questions about PET monitoring, Centiloid thresholds, pharmacodynamic response, p-tau217 change, treatment duration and the distinction between amyloid clearance and patient benefit.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The analysis uses a prespecified quantitative amyloid-PET threshold of less than 24.1 Centiloids to define clearance. It supports Centiloid-based pharmacodynamic interpretation but does not validate visual reads, establish interchangeability across tracers or scanners, or authorize PET or plasma biomarkers as surrogate clinical end points.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No authorization, availability, reimbursement or coverage change. Additional PET monitoring could carry cost and capacity implications, but this analysis did not establish a covered monitoring schedule.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Did amyloid clearance predict a larger clinical benefit?
Not clearly. CDR-SB slowing was similar in clear and non-clear subgroups, while iADRS slowing was numerically larger after clearance; the post-hoc analysis was not randomized by clearance status.
Does 24.1 Centiloids become a validated surrogate end point?
No. The threshold operationalized PET clearance in this analysis; the study does not establish regulatory surrogacy or an individual stopping rule.
Was plasma p-tau217 sufficient to replace PET?
No. Plasma p-tau217 changed with treatment, but the study did not validate it as an interchangeable measure of PET clearance or clinical benefit.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Post-hoc exploratory subgroup analysis
  • Clearance status was not randomized
  • Only participants with evaluable week-52 PET entered the clearance comparison
  • Matched-placebo analyses may retain residual confounding
  • No new prospective monitoring algorithm or clinical-utility test

Primary source · DOI

Shcherbinin S, Lu M, Wang J, et al. Post-hoc analyses of amyloid reduction after one year of treatment with donanemab using clinical trial data: prediction of amyloid clearance and association with downstream measurements. Alzheimers Res Ther. Published online October 16, 2026. doi:10.1186/s13195-026-02163-9.

Practice-relevant•Peer-reviewed multidisciplinary consensus recommendations•October 15, 2026

Italian intersocietal consensus specifies an anti-amyloid implementation pathway

Twenty-one Italian scientific societies and patient associations endorsed 36 operational statements that pair trial-aligned MRI eligibility and risk-adapted ARIA monitoring with a stepwise confirmation pathway using plasma biomarkers, automated CSF assays and amyloid PET.

Key recommendations: The panel evaluated 36 statements across five operational domains and reported strong agreement for the large majority.

BiomarkersGuidelinesManagementBloodAmyloidPlasma Alzheimer biomarkersBiological confirmation

Added October 16, 2026 · DOI:10.1016/j.tjpad.2026.100685; PMID:42880054

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The update translates European lecanemab and donanemab availability into a competence-based service model. It recommends harmonized CDR staging, a defined multidisciplinary team, trial-aligned MRI eligibility, risk-adapted ARIA monitoring and stepwise biomarker confirmation. Agreement was quantified through a modified Delphi process, but the source is consensus rather than a GRADE-based guideline or prospective utility study.

Evidence basis and population

After implementation gaps emerged from the panel's 2025 document, the Italian Expert Panel on Alzheimer reconvened 21 scientific societies and patient associations. A multidisciplinary panel rated 36 declarative statements across five domains: tiered cognitive-disorders services, clinical staging and monitoring, eligibility in MCI and atypical phenotypes, multidisciplinary-team composition, and MRI/ARIA/biomarker pathways.

Key recommendations

  • The panel evaluated 36 statements across five operational domains and reported strong agreement for the large majority.
  • The consensus recommends a competence-based reorganization of Italian cognitive-disorders centers and harmonized use of the Clinical Dementia Rating for staging and monitoring.
  • It endorses trial-aligned MRI eligibility criteria, a move toward risk-adapted ARIA monitoring, and a stepwise biomarker pathway integrating plasma assays, automated CSF platforms and amyloid PET.
  • The publication does not report formal GRADE certainty ratings or recommendation grades; its strength is quantified expert agreement from a modified Delphi process.

What changed

The Italian framework now addresses concrete operational gaps that appeared after European authorization, including how centers should be organized, how staging should be harmonized, and how blood, CSF, PET and MRI should be sequenced around treatment.

Strength of evidence

Multisociety consensus with a formal modified-Delphi method and broad stakeholder participation. Recommendations are operationally important but are not a substitute for drug labeling, national reimbursement rules, assay-specific validation or prospective clinical-utility evidence.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The document provides a practical blueprint for centers implementing anti-amyloid therapy in Italy, particularly for referral, confirmation, eligibility and ARIA surveillance. Local prescribing information and regional or national access rules remain controlling.

Field medical relevance

High value for MSL discussions about reflex testing, division of labor across laboratories and imaging services, atypical phenotypes, MRI thresholds, ARIA monitoring and the distinction between consensus, authorization and reimbursement.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The pathway is modality-specific but not product-specific: plasma tests are positioned within a stepwise pathway, automated CSF and amyloid PET provide biological confirmation, and MRI is used for eligibility and ARIA surveillance. The paper does not make assays or platforms interchangeable or establish new analytical-performance claims.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The framework is intended to support equitable and sustainable Italian access, but it does not itself create reimbursement, expand authorized indications or guarantee laboratory, PET or MRI capacity.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Is this a formal clinical practice guideline?
No. It is a final peer-reviewed intersocietal consensus produced with a modified Delphi process; the paper does not report GRADE-based recommendation strength.
Does it authorize plasma biomarkers as a stand-alone treatment test?
No. Plasma assays are incorporated into a stepwise pathway alongside automated CSF testing and amyloid PET, with clinical and imaging eligibility assessment still required.
Does it change reimbursement?
No. It offers a blueprint for prescribing centers and reimbursing authorities but is not itself a reimbursement or coverage decision.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Consensus rather than prospective implementation or outcomes evidence
  • Italian health-system context limits direct transfer to other jurisdictions
  • No formal GRADE certainty or recommendation-strength labels reported
  • Assay-specific cutoffs and analytical-performance requirements are not established by the consensus
  • Drug labels and payer rules remain separate

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Benussi A, Agosta F, Agnello L, et al. Updated Italian intersocietal recommendations for the appropriate use of anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies in Alzheimer's disease. J Prev Alzheimers Dis. Published online October 15, 2026. doi:10.1016/j.tjpad.2026.100685.

Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed anatomical-phantom technical validation•October 15, 2026

An anatomical phantom exposes material bias in uncorrected amyloid-PET quantification

Across simulated gray-to-white matter ratios, uncorrected amyloid-PET measures had mean absolute inaccuracies of 14.1% for tissue ratio and 19.8% for SUVR; partial-volume correction reduced them as low as 6.1% and 7.6%, with modified 3-compartment and GTM methods performing best.

Key quantitative results: Uncorrected gray-to-white ratio and SUVR had mean absolute inaccuracies of 14.1% and 19.8%, respectively.

BiomarkersAmyloid PETAmyloid PET SUVRPET quantification

Added October 16, 2026 · DOI:10.1186/s40658-026-00956-3

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Partial-volume effects can materially distort amyloid-PET SUVR, particularly when cortical atrophy or small structures mix gray and white matter signals. This phantom study shows that correction improves accuracy without a relevant loss of precision, but the best method still needs clinical validation on specific scanner, tracer and reconstruction combinations.

Study design

The StepBrain anatomical phantom was scanned to reproduce clinical amyloid-PET distributions across gray-to-white matter ratios from 0% to 120%. Atlas-based gray-to-white ratios and cerebellum-normalized SUVRs were calculated without correction and after 2-compartment, 3-compartment, modified 3-compartment and geometric transfer matrix correction. Linear mixed models compared accuracy and precision against the known phantom ground truth.

Key quantitative results

  • Uncorrected gray-to-white ratio and SUVR had mean absolute inaccuracies of 14.1% and 19.8%, respectively.
  • Partial-volume correction reduced mean absolute inaccuracy as low as 6.1% for gray-to-white ratio and 7.6% for SUVR.
  • Accuracy and precision differed significantly among methods for both measures (F>95 for all comparisons).
  • Three-compartment, modified 3-compartment and geometric transfer matrix correction improved tracer-ratio accuracy without relevant precision loss; modified 3-compartment and GTM were the most accurate and precise.

What changed

The study supplies a physical ground truth for comparing amyloid-PET partial-volume methods and quantifies how much uncorrected SUVR can be biased in clinically realistic uptake patterns.

Strength of evidence

Strong analytical-method evidence within a controlled phantom experiment, with direct ground truth and head-to-head methods. Clinical validity and utility remain unproven because a phantom cannot reproduce motion, biological heterogeneity, tracer kinetics, scanner diversity or patient-specific anatomy.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Quantitative amyloid-PET reports should identify whether and how partial-volume correction was applied, especially for longitudinal monitoring or low-burden decisions. The numerical results should not be used as a universal correction factor.

Field medical relevance

Useful for MSL and imaging discussions about SUVR bias, atrophy, longitudinal treatment monitoring, method harmonization and why quantitative pipelines require scanner- and tracer-specific validation.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The head-to-head phantom comparison provides a known ground truth for partial-volume bias. Modified 3-compartment and geometric transfer matrix approaches were most accurate and precise in this setup, but results do not establish universal equivalence across scanners, reconstructions, tracers, atlases or patient anatomy.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No access or coverage change. More advanced correction may require software, expertise and harmonized quality control that are not uniformly available.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Should every amyloid PET scan use the best-performing method from this study?
Not automatically. Modified 3-compartment and GTM performed best in this phantom, but each clinical pipeline needs validation for its tracer, scanner, reconstruction, atlas and patient population.
Does partial-volume correction eliminate bias?
No. It reduced mean absolute inaccuracy substantially but did not reduce it to zero.
Was clinical utility tested?
No. The study measured technical accuracy and precision, not diagnostic decisions, treatment selection or patient outcomes.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Phantom rather than patient data
  • Does not reproduce motion, biological heterogeneity or tracer kinetics
  • Single experimental imaging and processing setup
  • No clinical decision thresholds or outcomes
  • No authorization, guideline or coverage assessment

Primary source · DOI

Pirozzi MA, Di Giorgio E, Prinster A, et al. Application of an anatomical brain phantom in the evaluation of partial volume effect correction of amyloid PET studies. EJNMMI Phys. Published online October 15, 2026. doi:10.1186/s40658-026-00956-3.

Important new evidence•FDA 510(k) decision summary•October 8, 2025

FDA cleared Elecsys pTau181 Plasma as a primary-care rule-out aid

At 13.1% amyloid-PET prevalence, the single 0.722 pg/mL cutoff produced 92.7% positive agreement, 51.3% negative agreement, 97.9% NPV, and 22.4% PPV in 312 primary-care patients.

Key label details: At the 0.722 pg/mL cutoff, positive percent agreement was 92.7% (38/41; 95% CI, 80.6%–97.5%) and negative percent agreement was 51.3% (139/271; 95% CI, 45.4%–57.2%).

BiomarkersBloodp-tau181Rule-out triage

Added October 20, 2026 · FDA 510(k) K252163

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The clearance is intentionally asymmetric. A negative result is consistent with a negative amyloid PET and may reduce unnecessary imaging, but nearly half of PET-negative participants tested positive. The FDA summary therefore supports rule-out triage, not standalone confirmation, and shows how low prevalence drives high NPV and low PPV.

Study design

FDA reviewed analytical validation and a pivotal clinical study in 312 evaluable primary-care patients aged at least 55 years who presented with cognitive concerns or impairment. The plasma result at a prespecified 0.722 pg/mL cutoff was compared with majority visual amyloid-PET classification; 41/312 participants were PET positive.

Key label details

  • At the 0.722 pg/mL cutoff, positive percent agreement was 92.7% (38/41; 95% CI, 80.6%–97.5%) and negative percent agreement was 51.3% (139/271; 95% CI, 45.4%–57.2%).
  • At 13.1% amyloid-PET prevalence, NPV was 97.9% (139/142; 95% CI, 94.0%–99.3%) and PPV was 22.4% (38/170; 95% CI, 19.5%–25.0%).
  • Three of 41 PET-positive patients tested negative, while 132 of 271 PET-negative patients tested positive.
  • FDA estimated that negative testing could reduce unnecessary amyloid PET by 45.5% (142/312).
  • The measuring range was 0.300–50.00 pg/mL; no high-dose hook effect was observed through 150 pg/mL.

What changed

This historical criteria-repair entry documents a previously unbriefed FDA-cleared automated p-tau181 rule-out assay and its markedly prevalence-dependent predictive values.

Strength of evidence

High regulatory and analytical-validity evidence with public pivotal performance data. Clinical utility is limited to the cleared initial-assessment aid; prospective patient-outcome benefit, specialty-care use, prognosis, and serial monitoring were not established.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

A negative result can support ruling out amyloid pathology in primary care, but a positive result cannot confirm amyloid pathology and should trigger further evaluation. The intended population and low-prevalence setting are integral to interpretation.

Field medical relevance

Provides a concrete comparison point for p-tau217 assays and illustrates why intended use, cutoff architecture, prevalence, PPV, NPV, and referral setting must be separated when discussing blood tests.

Quanterix or platform relevance

This is a fully automated electrochemiluminescence assay with an 18-minute run time and a single negative/positive cutoff. Its intended role differs from three-zone p-tau217 workflows: the high NPV supports rule-out in low-prevalence primary care, while the low PPV means positive results need further investigation.

Access or reimbursement relevance

FDA clearance establishes authorization, not universal laboratory availability, payer coverage, reimbursement, or guideline endorsement. Local ordering and payment require separate verification.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Can a positive result confirm Alzheimer disease?
No. PPV was 22.4% in the pivotal primary-care cohort, and the FDA labeling says positive results should be investigated further.
Can the assay be used in specialty clinics?
Its cleared intended use is initial assessment, and the summary states it is not recommended for patients already referred to a specialist.
Can it monitor therapy or predict dementia?
No. Those uses were not established in the cleared labeling.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Historical criteria-repair backfill rather than a newly source-dated development
  • Low amyloid prevalence produced very low PPV
  • Single binary cutoff leaves many false-positive results
  • Intended use is limited to initial assessment outside specialty care
  • No prognostic, treatment-monitoring, or patient-outcome utility claim

Primary source · FDA 510(k) record

U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Elecsys Phospho-Tau (181P) Plasma. 510(k) K252163. Decision October 8, 2025.

Implementation-relevant•Peer-reviewed retrospective real-world imaging study•October 8, 2026

Real-world lecanemab PET monitoring reveals visual-quantitative discordance

In 38 amyloid-PET-positive patients treated for 6–8 months, amyloid burden fell by 29.39±22.31 Centiloids, but visual and quantitative response agreement was poor to fair (κ 0.205–0.253), supporting explicit Centiloid quantification for serial monitoring rather than visual interpretation alone.

Key quantitative results: Mean amyloid reduction was 29.39±22.31 Centiloids (p<0.001); MMSE, MoCA and tau-PET measures did not change significantly.

BiomarkersAmyloid PETAmyloid CentiloidTau PET SUVRTreatment response monitoring

Added October 16, 2026 · DOI:10.1177/13872877261493063

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The cohort shows substantial short-term plaque reduction without measurable cognitive or tau-PET change. Only 12 of 38 reached less than 24.1 Centiloids and five were visually negative. The discordance supports quantitative serial assessment when PET is obtained, but this small uncontrolled cohort cannot prove clinical utility or determine when treatment should stop.

Study design

Investigators retrospectively analyzed 38 amyloid-PET-positive patients with Alzheimer disease who received lecanemab for 6–8 months. Paired tests evaluated Centiloid and cognitive change, kappa measured visual-quantitative agreement, and exploratory regression assessed predictors of amyloid reduction.

Key quantitative results

  • Mean amyloid reduction was 29.39±22.31 Centiloids (p<0.001); MMSE, MoCA and tau-PET measures did not change significantly.
  • Twelve of 38 patients reached less than 24.1 Centiloids, while only five were visually negative.
  • Visual-quantitative agreement was poor to fair: κ=0.205 for positivity and κ=0.253 for treatment efficacy.
  • Baseline Centiloid burden (standardized β=0.594, p<0.001) and number of treatment cycles (β=0.285, p=0.022) independently predicted greater clearance; tau SUVR had a marginal inverse association (β=-0.238, p=0.052). The multivariable model adjusted R² was 0.507.

What changed

This real-world study directly quantifies the gap between visual and Centiloid-based interpretation during short-term lecanemab therapy and proposes a hybrid screening-and-monitoring workflow.

Strength of evidence

Early real-world evidence with paired PET and quantitative effect estimates, but retrospective, uncontrolled and limited to 38 patients. Visual-reading methods, tracer/scanner generalizability and downstream clinical utility require independent validation.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

If serial amyloid PET is obtained, visual negativity alone may miss low residual burden and quantitative Centiloid reporting can add interpretive precision. The study does not establish that routine serial PET improves outcomes or should guide dose changes.

Field medical relevance

Addresses recurring MSL questions about visual versus quantitative reads, low-burden discordance, Centiloid thresholds and PET-based response monitoring under anti-amyloid therapy.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The central comparison is visual versus quantitative amyloid-PET interpretation during lecanemab treatment. Poor agreement indicates that visual and Centiloid assessments are not interchangeable near low residual burden; the study did not validate performance across tracers, scanners or independent readers.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No authorization or coverage change. Serial quantitative PET could increase imaging demand and cost; the study did not evaluate reimbursement or access.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does the study establish routine serial PET monitoring?
No. It shows measurement discordance in a small cohort but did not test whether serial PET improves treatment decisions or outcomes.
Can visual negativity and less than 24.1 Centiloids be treated as equivalent?
No. Twelve patients crossed the quantitative threshold while only five were visually negative, and kappa agreement was low.
Did plaque reduction produce short-term cognitive improvement?
No significant MMSE or MoCA change was detected over 6–8 months.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Historical criteria-repair backfill rather than a newly published item
  • Retrospective single-cohort design
  • Only 38 patients
  • No untreated comparator
  • Short 6–8-month follow-up
  • No validation across tracers, scanners or independent readers
  • No clinical-utility or patient-outcome analysis

Primary source · DOI

Qiao Z, Zhao X, Wang G, et al. PET-based evaluation of short-term amyloid-β clearance and predictive factors in real-world Alzheimer's disease patients treated with lecanemab. J Alzheimers Dis. Published online October 8, 2026. doi:10.1177/13872877261493063.

Important new evidence•Peer-reviewed autopsy-confirmed PET-pathology study•September 23, 2026

Autopsy validation shows late-stage flortaucipir uptake differs across primary cortex

Among 155 autopsy-confirmed Alzheimer cases, flortaucipir uptake in primary isocortices began at Braak stage V, with visual and auditory regions increasing earlier and faster than motor and somatosensory regions.

Key quantitative results: The analysis included 155 autopsy-confirmed participants with Alzheimer disease.

BiomarkersTau PETFlortaucipir tau PETBraak neurofibrillary tangle stageBiological staging

Added October 16, 2026 · DOI:10.1016/j.isci.2026.117530; PMID:42830961; PMCID:PMC13634365

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

Primary isocortex is usually emphasized as the terminal Braak stage, but uptake was not uniform. Visual and auditory cortex showed earlier and steeper flortaucipir increases than motor and somatosensory cortex, and age and APOE ε4 influenced uptake. The result refines late-stage spatial interpretation without validating a new treatment-selection threshold.

Study design

Researchers measured flortaucipir uptake in primary visual, auditory, motor and somatosensory isocortices in 155 participants with autopsy-confirmed Alzheimer disease, then related regional uptake to neuropathologic Braak stage and clinical or genetic covariates.

Key quantitative results

  • The analysis included 155 autopsy-confirmed participants with Alzheimer disease.
  • Flortaucipir uptake in primary isocortices became apparent beginning at Braak stage V.
  • Visual and auditory isocortices showed greater and faster uptake increases than somatosensory and motor cortex.
  • Age and APOE ε4 influenced uptake; primary-isocortex patterns resembled lateral temporal cortex more than entorhinal cortex.

What changed

The pathology-anchored analysis shows that primary cortical regions do not behave as one homogeneous late-stage tau-PET compartment and that visual/auditory regions may signal advanced spread earlier than traditionally emphasized.

Strength of evidence

Moderate-to-strong clinical-validity evidence because diagnosis and Braak stage were autopsy confirmed and the cohort was sizeable for pathology studies. The analysis remains cross-sectional and tracer-specific, and clinical utility was not tested.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

Regional late-stage flortaucipir interpretation may need to distinguish visual and auditory cortex from motor and somatosensory cortex. The findings do not create a new authorized stage, threshold or treatment-eligibility rule.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to tau-PET visual and quantitative staging, spatial reporting, pathology concordance and discussions of how late-stage regional uptake should be interpreted.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The study links regional flortaucipir uptake to neuropathologically confirmed Braak stage. It supports regional interpretation for this tracer but does not establish equivalence with other tau tracers, visual-staging schemes or quantitative pipelines.

Access or reimbursement relevance

No new availability or coverage change. The study may inform specialist interpretation but does not expand access to tau PET.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does uptake in primary cortex define a new clinical stage?
No. The study refines regional relationships with neuropathologic Braak stage but does not validate a new clinical staging system.
Can the pattern be generalized to every tau tracer?
No. The evidence is specific to flortaucipir and requires tracer-specific replication.
Was treatment eligibility or response tested?
No. This was a PET-pathology interpretation study.
